title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
authors: Peter Sharpe, Carmelo Gonzales, Corey Adams, Mehdi Ataei, Sanjay Choudhry
abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

infographic.key_insight: AeroZoo shows that encoding boundary conditions can sharply improve aerodynamic flow prediction, while unseen enclosures and boundary-condition layouts remain major generalization challenges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark tests whether fast CFD surrogates can predict flows across new shapes and enclosures, rather than only within a single design family.
method: Generate 3,815 time-mean unsteady RANS solutions with a transition model across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from 10³ to 10⁸.
Specify each problem using boundary meshes grouped by condition type, prescribed values and fluid properties.
Evaluate two tasks with engineering metrics and 22 frozen, geometry-disjoint splits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 2,816 stable-mean cases used for benchmarking, boundary-condition tokens reduced GeoTransolver’s random-split median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of inlet speed in single-seed runs; ISLA reached 5.3% over four seeds.
infographic.watch_item: Held-out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts increased ISLA’s error 2.4–9.2 times, cautioning against assuming reliable deployment in unfamiliar flow domains.
infographic.paper_title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics

title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Vortex-Induced Instability Over a Semi-Infinite Flat Plate with Discrete Roughness
authors: Aditi Sengupta, Tapan K. Sengupta, Vajjala K. Suman
abstract: The receptivity of flow over a semi-infinite flat plate to a combination of deterministic free stream excitation and surface roughness, is investigated by solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation (NSE). The free stream excitation is in the form of a convecting vortex with fixed strength and sign, while the roughness element is a Gaussian bump. Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed to determine whether the nonmodal nonlinear nature of transition, previously established for the vortex-induced instability in [Sundaram et al., Effects of free stream excitation on the boundary layer over a semi-infinite flat plate, Phys. Fluids, 32, 094110 (2020))], holds in the presence of surface roughness. The study aims to capture the fundamental differences arising due to the addition of surface roughness using instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics and application of nonlinear theories of receptivity. Roughness accelerates the transition process significantly, while retaining the indicator of nonmodal response, i.e. the spatio-temporal wave front (STWF). The inherently 2D nature of the vortex-induced instability evolves to three-dimensionality much faster in the presence of roughness, necessitating a 3D framework to capture the effects of roughness accurately. The cumulative response to the surface bump and convecting vortex can be separated into four stages, viz. are (i) generation of vortical disturbances at the roughness, (ii) a spatio-temporal amplification of the disturbance field, (iii) emergence and amplification of the STWF marked by sequence of unsteady separation bubbles, and (iv) emergence of turbulent flow due to merging of the unsteady separation bubbles to turbulent spots.

infographic.key_insight: A Gaussian surface bump significantly accelerates vortex-induced transition and three-dimensional development while preserving the spatio-temporal wave front characteristic of a nonmodal response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting boundary-layer transition under combined surface roughness and free-stream vortices requires accounting for their interaction and rapid development of three-dimensional flow.
method: Solve the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations using 2D and 3D direct numerical simulations.
Combine a convecting vortex of fixed strength and sign with a Gaussian bump on a semi-infinite flat plate.
Analyze instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics, and nonlinear receptivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations identify four stages: roughness-generated disturbances, spatio-temporal amplification, wave-front emergence with unsteady separation bubbles, and bubble merging into turbulent spots.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative transition shifts or parameter ranges, so generalization beyond the prescribed vortex and Gaussian bump remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Vortex-Induced Instability Over a Semi-Infinite Flat Plate with Discrete Roughness

title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
authors: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang
abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

infographic.key_insight: Gradient-aware AI agents autonomously discover and train turbulence closures by combining LLM-guided model design with gradients from differentiable CFD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce manual effort in developing turbulence closures tailored to target flow statistics.
method: Use a multi-agent LLM system to propose analytical, neural, or hybrid closure forms.
Embed closures and objectives in a GPU-native differentiable CFD solver and validate gradient paths.
Use simulation feedback and truncated-horizon gradients to optimize parameters and revise proposals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests span dissipation laws and subgrid-scale closures in 2D turbulence and wall models for 3D channel-flow LES; gradient-based training recovers reference coefficients not reached by forward evaluation alone within the same budget.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the demonstrated flows remains unestablished, and chaotic dynamics require careful selection of gradient truncation horizons.
infographic.paper_title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD

title: Resolvent-based modeling of turbulent flow over multilayer compliant surfaces
authors: Rutvij Bhagwat, Kourosh Shoele
abstract: Compliant coatings offer a passive approach to modifying near-wall turbulence and potentially reducing skin-friction drag, but high-fidelity exploration of the coupled parameter space is costly. We develop a two-way coupled resolvent-Galerkin framework for turbulent channel flow over finite-thickness, layered viscoelastic coatings. The fluid is modeled using the Navier-Stokes equations linearized about a turbulent mean state, while the solid is represented by a through-thickness Galerkin discretization of the elastodynamic equations. The solid response is condensed into a spectral surface-impedance operator at the fluid-solid interface. At $Re_τ= 180$, stiff panels approach the rigid-wall response, whereas more compliant panels modify the low-rank response associated with the near-wall cycle. A Reynolds-number study shows that panels with fixed nondimensional material stiffness can produce different responses depending on whether their thickness scales with inner or outer flow length scales. The influence of viscoelastic damping is examined across low- and high-frequency regimes, where stiffness-proportional damping alters the high-frequency fractional-energy distribution, while the low-frequency distribution remains relatively insensitive to damping. For multilayer panels, the fluid-facing material determines the interfacial wave speed, while the subsurface stiffness distribution modifies the panel's effective thickness. Temporal stability analysis identifies regions of parameter space where a steady harmonic response is relevant and regions where instabilities grow. Finally, a leading-order, covariance-based drag-estimation framework relates the coupled response to changes in the mean flow and to the estimated skin-friction drag. Together, these tools provide a basis for screening coating designs and selecting candidates for high-fidelity simulations and experiments.

infographic.key_insight: Layered compliant coatings reshape near-wall turbulent responses through surface stiffness, subsurface structure, thickness scaling, and damping.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables lower-cost screening of passive coating designs for potential skin-friction reduction before high-fidelity simulations or experiments.
method: Couple linearized fluid resolvent analysis with a through-thickness solid Galerkin model.
Represent layered viscoelastic coatings through a spectral surface-impedance operator.
Assess temporal stability and estimate drag changes using leading-order response covariances.
infographic.evidence_signal: At Reτ = 180, stiff panels approach rigid-wall behavior while more compliant panels modify near-wall low-rank responses; additional studies examine Reynolds-number scaling, damping, and layering.
infographic.watch_item: Drag changes are model-based estimates rather than demonstrated reductions, and unstable parameter regimes limit the relevance of steady harmonic responses.
infographic.paper_title: Resolvent-based modeling of turbulent flow over multilayer compliant surfaces

title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow
authors: Christophe Brouzet, Mayank Chopra, Dario Vincenzi, Jason R. Picardo, Atul Varshney
abstract: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.

infographic.key_insight: Experiments reveal a center-mode elastic instability at vanishing inertia in confined viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, showing that curved base-flow streamlines are not required.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This instability could enable enhanced mixing in low-inertia microfluidic, porous-media, and polymer-processing flows.
method: Drive confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow electromagnetically.
Observe velocity-field structures as forcing strength increases.
Use Oldroyd-B simulations to connect confined-flow dynamics to unbounded-flow center modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments show arrow-shaped velocity structures and increasingly chaotic fluctuations, reproduced in Oldroyd-B simulations and linked to travelling center-mode arrowheads.
infographic.watch_item: Generality beyond the confined quasi-two-dimensional setup and the Oldroyd-B model remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow

title: Gas expansion in global models of nanosecond pulsed discharges: a reduced gas-dynamic model coupled to plasma kinetics
authors: Konstantinos Kourtzanidis, Rention Pasolari
abstract: Global (zero-dimensional) kinetic models of nanosecond pulsed discharges describe the expansion of the heated gas channel (kernel) with simplified gas-dynamic closures. We show that these closures can lead to errors of tens of percent in the calculated gas density, temperature and species densities, especially in the first microseconds after every pulse. Here, we propose a fast, reduced gas-dynamic model of Lagrangian shells, closed by an approximate cylindrical acoustic radiation condition, with no fitted physical coefficient. The reduced model reproduces the axis density obtained by verified one- dimensional compressible computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations within 2.4% for smooth deposition profiles and axis pressures up to six times ambient, typically a thousand times faster than CFD. We couple it with our in-house global plasma-kinetics solver (SoPlasma-0D), whose energy partition after the pulse agrees well with that derived from measurements and with an independent calculation. Two microseconds after a single pulse in air, and compared with the proposed coupled model, the existing closures overestimate the axis density by up to a factor of 2.8, the atomic oxygen density by up to 2.7 and the temperature by up to 680 K. For repetitive pulses 200 or 430 ns apart, of equal energy per unit volume, no existing closure follows the coupled model at both intervals, in the gas density met by each later pulse and in the energy per molecule deposited by late pulses, which sets how strongly they dissociate and heat the gas. The proposed reduced model should therefore be used to describe the gas evolution during the expansion phase after every nanosecond pulse, and for repetitive pulses above about 100 kHz in kernels of radius up to about a millimetre.

infographic.key_insight: A fast reduced gas-dynamic model captures post-pulse gas expansion more accurately than existing closures, which can substantially overestimate density, temperature and reactive species.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved expansion modeling helps predict the gas density and energy per molecule encountered by successive pulses in high-repetition-rate plasma systems.
method: Represent radial gas expansion with Lagrangian shells.
Close the model with an approximate cylindrical acoustic radiation condition, without fitted physical coefficients.
Couple gas dynamics to the SoPlasma-0D global plasma-kinetics solver.
infographic.evidence_signal: For smooth deposition profiles and axis pressures up to six times ambient, the reduced model reproduces verified 1D compressible CFD axis densities within 2.4%, typically running about 1,000 times faster.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the tested smooth deposition profiles and pressure range requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Gas expansion in global models of nanosecond pulsed discharges: a reduced gas-dynamic model coupled to plasma kinetics

title: Graph Neural Network based non-local models: Toward application to RANS turbulence modeling
authors: Salvatore Civiello, Davide Oberto, Antonia Larese, Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: Most machine-learning closures for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations are local, predicting the closure quantities at each point solely from local flow features, despite the non-local nature of turbulent interactions. We propose a non-local closure framework based on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) that exploits the mesh connectivity. Each finite-volume cell becomes a graph node, and cells sharing a face are connected by an edge. Through message passing, each layer aggregates information from neighboring nodes, so that after $k$ layers the prediction at a cell depends on its $k$-hop neighborhood, which naturally accounts for non-local effects. To make training feasible when each simulation yields a single large graph, we also introduce a breadth-first-search $k$-hop subgraph sampling strategy, which acts as data augmentation and cuts the cost per processed graph during training. We compare GCNs with feed-forward networks (FNNs) of equal size on two periodic-hills benchmarks: a laminar advection-diffusion transport problem that mimics the non-local character of RANS closures, and the turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction of the Closure Challenge dataset at $Re = 5600$. In the laminar case, FNNs are accurate only within the training regime and with sufficiently informative inputs, whereas GCNs generalize better to unseen geometries, including out-of-distribution flows, and partly compensate for missing input features. In the turbulent proof-of-concept case, the graph-based models achieve modest but consistent improvements compared to FNNs, supporting GCNs as a promising route to non-local RANS closures.

infographic.key_insight: Mesh-based graph neural networks capture neighborhood information, improving on local neural models for non-local closure prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Using existing finite-volume mesh connectivity offers a practical route toward RANS closures that account for surrounding flow conditions.
method: Represent finite-volume cells as nodes and shared faces as graph edges.
Use GCN message passing so k layers incorporate information from k-hop neighborhoods.
Train on breadth-first-search k-hop subgraphs to augment data and reduce per-graph processing cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against equal-size feed-forward networks, GCNs generalize better in a laminar periodic-hills transport benchmark and show modest, consistent gains in turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction at Re = 5600.
infographic.watch_item: The turbulent result is a proof of concept for eddy-viscosity prediction, not evidence of improved coupled RANS simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Neural Network based non-local models: Toward application to RANS turbulence modeling

title: An LLM-assisted theoretical model for aeroengine installation noise scattering
authors: Xun Huang
abstract: A theoretical model is developed for the canonical problem of aeroengine fan noise impinging on, and scattering from, a nearby semi-infinite rigid plate. The model chains two Wiener--Hopf problems in different coordinate systems. The first stage solves the duct-radiation problem analytically in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates. The second stage expands the field incident on the plate into a double angular spectrum of plane waves: the axial spectrum is inherited from the first stage, while the spanwise spectrum is generated by a Weyl--Sommerfeld expansion of the cylindrical harmonics. Each spectral component is then scattered by the plate. The mathematical crux is the coordinate transformation between the axisymmetric duct frame and the Cartesian plate frame. The core physical insight--that the Weyl--Sommerfeld identity provides an exact spectral bridge between these systems--originates entirely with the authors. The heavy algebra of translating between the two spectral representations, together with the associated numerical verification, was carried out with the assistance of a large language model (LLM), under strict human oversight and independent numerical cross-checking. This division of labour enables the LLM to handle tedious symbolic manipulation without compromising rigour. Results are presented for spinning modes radiating from a cylindrical duct with a subsonic jet into a quiescent ambient. The case study demonstrates that, under systematic verification, LLMs can accelerate tedious algebra in theoretical fluid mechanics, contributing a concrete empirical example to the broader discussion on AI's role in theoretical research.

infographic.key_insight: The Weyl–Sommerfeld identity exactly connects cylindrical duct acoustics to Cartesian plate-scattering spectra, enabling a chained theoretical model of aeroengine installation noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports analysis of how fan noise radiating from an engine duct scatters from a nearby rigid surface.
method: Solve duct radiation analytically using a cylindrical-coordinate Wiener–Hopf formulation.
Use the Weyl–Sommerfeld expansion to transform cylindrical harmonics into a double angular spectrum, then solve plate scattering.
Use an LLM for algebraic translation and numerical verification under human oversight and independent cross-checking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports results for spinning duct modes with a subsonic jet in a quiescent ambient and independent numerical cross-checking, but gives no quantitative accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The canonical semi-infinite rigid plate idealization limits direct transfer to finite, geometrically complex aircraft surfaces.
infographic.paper_title: An LLM-assisted theoretical model for aeroengine installation noise scattering

title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
authors: Yingqi Hu, Nan Deng, Changxiao Shao, Xiaozhou He
abstract: Data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, and hierarchical U-shaped networks, which resemble the structure of classical Geometric Multigrid (GMG) methods, have become prevalent designs. Modern surrogates built on these designs achieve competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers; however, accurate prediction of complex flows remains challenging, and no existing architecture leads across them. In such networks, the multigrid analogy mainly concerns the multi-resolution topology, while their components largely follow common vision practice. To address this, this study introduces SUMNO, a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow fields on regular grids that spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. Parameter-free down- and upsampling stand in for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, with normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Within this macro-architecture, convolutions are used at the fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, whose window partitioning is generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis. Evaluated on unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five representative baselines, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and ranks second in the remaining two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters using 9.4 million parameters.

infographic.key_insight: SUMNO turns a multigrid V-cycle into a U-shaped neural operator, combining strong flow-prediction accuracy with a compact 9.4-million-parameter model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SUMNO offers a parameter-efficient approach to regular-grid CFD surrogates for steady-flow prediction and unsteady-flow rollouts.
method: Spatially unrolls a multigrid V-cycle using parameter-free downsampling and upsampling with additive skip corrections.
Keeps transfer and skip pathways normalization-free.
Combines fine- and intermediate-grid convolutions with coarse-grid shifted-window attention supporting periodicity independently per axis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow benchmarks and five baselines on unseen test configurations, SUMNO ranks first in 5 of 7 settings and second in two, with about 30% lower 10-step rollout MSE than the strongest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to regular-grid benchmarks; performance on irregular meshes and stability over longer rollouts remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates

title: Scale-aware composite forcing enhances forward energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence
authors: Hongxuan Zhang, Fanxi Gong, Yating Chen, Runchao Guan
abstract: In forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (FHIT), conventional large-scale forcing sustains statistical stationarity but offers limited control over energy at intermediate scales. We propose a scale-aware composite forcing strategy for the lattice Boltzmann method, combining large-scale random forcing with feedback aligned with an intermediate-scale velocity field extracted by composite filtering. The magnitude of the cross-power spectrum between feedback and filtered velocity is concentrated in the target band, with a time-averaged fraction of 72.26%-74.56%. Feedback increases energy in both target and high-wavenumber bands, with larger relative gains at high wavenumbers. At feedback strengths $α$ = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, the target-band energy fraction increases by 6.29%, 11.65%, 18.99%, and 19.89% relative to the baseline. The mean forward nonlinear energy flux across K = 12 rises to 1.18, 1.54, 2.32, and 3.06 times its baseline value, with larger relative increases than across K = 4. As $α$ increases from 0% to 7%, the mean Taylor-microscale Reynolds number rises from 73.94 to 97.86 and enstrophy increases by 181.98%, while longitudinal velocity-gradient skewness shifts toward zero and standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions largely retain their shapes. Mean $k_{\max}η$ values of 1.01 and 0.90 at 5% and 7% feedback indicate an approaching resolution limit and a risk of under-resolution, respectively. At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback gives a target-band energy fraction of 32.36%, versus 27.55% under enhanced large-scale forcing, and a post-transient forward flux across K = 12 generally 2.17-2.39 times larger. The strategy thus enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear transfer, with feedback strength constrained by small-scale resolution.

infographic.key_insight: Scale-aware composite forcing targets intermediate-scale motion and strengthens forward nonlinear energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann turbulence simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers finer control of turbulent energy distribution than large-scale forcing alone, provided small-scale resolution remains adequate.
method: Combine large-scale random forcing with intermediate-scale velocity-aligned feedback.
Extract the target velocity field using composite filtering.
Compare feedback strengths of 1%–7% against baseline and enhanced large-scale forcing.
infographic.evidence_signal: At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback yields a 32.36% target-band energy fraction versus 27.55% for enhanced large-scale forcing, with 2.17–2.39 times greater post-transient forward flux across K = 12.
infographic.watch_item: Mean k_maxη falls to 1.01 at 5% feedback and 0.90 at 7%, indicating an approaching resolution limit and under-resolution risk, respectively.
infographic.paper_title: Scale-aware composite forcing enhances forward energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence

title: On the relation of secondary motions to large- and very-large-scale motions
authors: Kay Schäfer
abstract: The coexistence of secondary motions with large-scale and very-large-scale motions (LSMs/VLSMs) is investigated by direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges, varying the ridge spacing $S$ and height $h$. First, the ridge height controls the secondary-motion strength and thereby the coexistence with VLSMs. VLSMs are suppressed for $h \geqslant 0.05δ$, with $δ$ the open-channel height, and re-emerge at $h = 0.025δ$, where the mean secondary motions are comparable in strength to those over strip-type surfaces. Previously reported differences between strip- and ridge-type surfaces thus reflect secondary-motion strength rather than surface type. Second, proper orthogonal decomposition and conditional averaging reveal instantaneous secondary motions that span approximately $2δ$, fill the channel height irrespective of $S$ and $h$, and are stronger than their mean. These are identified as LSMs spatially locked and amplified by the ridges. Over dense ridges, their alternation between neighbouring ridges yields weak, near-wall confined mean secondary motions, although VLSMs are suppressed over the full channel height. The ridge height thus sets the strength of the locked LSMs, whereas the ridge spacing sets where and for how long they persist. For weak locked LSMs, ridges spaced at their natural spanwise extent increase the VLSM energy, indicating that persistent locked LSMs concatenate into VLSMs. Third, large-scale instantaneous secondary motions persist over dense ridges in the absence of long streaks. This suggests that secondary motions are driven by intermittent cross-sectional motions rather than by long streaks, similar to the streak-less bursts in near-wall turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Secondary motions are ridge-locked, amplified large-scale motions whose strength governs coexistence with very-large-scale motions, while ridge spacing controls their location and persistence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ridge height and spacing offer design levers for tuning large-scale turbulence organization over patterned channel surfaces.
method: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges.
Variation of ridge height and spacing.
Proper orthogonal decomposition and conditional averaging of instantaneous motions.
infographic.evidence_signal: VLSMs were suppressed at ridge heights h ≥ 0.05δ and re-emerged at h = 0.025δ, while instantaneous secondary motions spanned approximately 2δ and filled the channel height across the tested geometries.
infographic.watch_item: The reported thresholds apply to the simulated open-channel configurations; transfer to other flow conditions or surface geometries requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: On the relation of secondary motions to large- and very-large-scale motions

title: Surrogate-Based Optimization of Tandem Twin-Rotor Wind Turbines Accounting for Wake Interactions
authors: Yinong Tian, Shan Wang
abstract: Wake interaction in a tandem twin-rotor turbine couples power capture with thrust on the shared support. This study develops a time-resolved surrogate for upstream IEA Wind 22 MW and downstream NREL 5 MW rotors. It covers spacing ratios $0.01\leq L/D\leq0.20$ and tip-speed ratios $4\leqλ\leq11$. Vortex-method simulations of 160 configurations under turbulent inflow train per-time-node XGBoost models to predict 600 s power, thrust, and torque histories. A CNN-Attention-LSTM network extends these histories, and a genetic algorithm balances the system power and thrust coefficients. Ten-fold cross-validation gives median power-history $R^2$ values of 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream for unseen configurations, but the first stage cannot extrapolate in tip-speed ratio. With fixed pitch and prescribed rotor speed, the coefficients apply where both rotors reach the simulated tip-speed ratio below rated wind speed. Increasing spacing raises upstream power by up to 6% and lowers downstream power by up to 62%. System power changes by less than 4% at fixed $λ$. The high-power end of the Pareto front lies near $λ=10$. At $L/D=0.20$, the system power coefficient is highest. This configuration has the lowest peak thrust among the high-power candidates.

infographic.key_insight: Wake-aware optimization favors high-power operation near λ = 10, with L/D = 0.20 delivering the highest system power coefficient and lowest peak thrust among high-power candidates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate supports power–thrust trade-off analysis for tandem twin-rotor turbines sharing a support structure.
method: Simulate 160 configurations under turbulent inflow using a vortex method.
Predict 600 s power, thrust, and torque histories with per-time-node XGBoost models, then extend them with CNN-Attention-LSTM.
Use a genetic algorithm to balance system power and thrust coefficients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ten-fold cross-validation on unseen configurations yielded median power-history R² values of 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream.
infographic.watch_item: The first-stage surrogate cannot extrapolate in tip-speed ratio; coefficients apply to fixed-pitch, prescribed-speed operation where both rotors attain the simulated ratio below rated wind speed.
infographic.paper_title: Surrogate-Based Optimization of Tandem Twin-Rotor Wind Turbines Accounting for Wake Interactions

title: Active flow control based on topological data analysis and a DMDc reduced-order model for drag reduction
authors: Constantini Mbangue Lobe Yiphta, Dina Razafindralandy
abstract: Controlling and reducing undesirable vortical structures in unsteady flows is a major issue in aerodynamics. This paper presents an active control methodology that combines topological data analysis (TDA) through persistence diagrams, a reduced-order model based on dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) and receding-horizon model predictive control (MPC). Vortices are detected and characterised by the persistence diagram of the absolute value of the vorticity, which makes it possible to define a target flow in which only the useful vortices are retained. This target flow is computed offline in the reduced space by gradient descent, the derivative of a persistence diagram being defined through a parametrisation of the space of diagrams. The control loop then reduces to a small-dimensional convex quadratic program, whose construction we detail and whose cost we compare with that of an approach that places the diagrams directly in the cost function. The approach is applied numerically to the flow around an oscillating aircraft wing for seven vibration frequencies, and yields a mean reduction of the drag coefficient while preserving the main vortices.

infographic.key_insight: Topology-guided flow targets combined with a DMDc reduced-order model and model predictive control reduce mean drag while retaining the main vortices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a computationally compact strategy for active aerodynamic flow control around an oscillating wing.
method: Detect and characterize vortices using persistence diagrams of absolute vorticity.
Compute a target flow offline by gradient descent in reduced space, retaining useful vortices.
Track the target with DMDc-based receding-horizon MPC solved as a small-dimensional convex quadratic program.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests around an oscillating aircraft wing at seven vibration frequencies report reduced mean drag coefficient while preserving the main vortices.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is numerical; robustness to experimental noise and operating conditions beyond the tested frequencies remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Active flow control based on topological data analysis and a DMDc reduced-order model for drag reduction

title: A conditional quadrature method of moments for populations of oblate spheroidal particles
authors: Mohamed Amine Bouguezzoul, Bianca Viggiano, Bruno Blais, Fabian Denner
abstract: Non-spherical particle populations are encountered in numerous industrial processes, where particle size, shape, and velocity jointly influence transport, breakage, and classification dynamics. The resulting coupled distributions of geometric and kinematic particle properties evolve within a high-dimensional phase space whose accurate representation remains a significant challenge. We present a conditional quadrature method of moments (CQMOM) for oblate spheroidal particles described by a five-dimensional phase space that includes their size, aspect ratio, and velocity. The dimensionality of the problem is reduced by assuming that the particles continuously adopt their drag-maximizing orientation. In the solution algorithm, the resulting conditional quadrature representation of the particle phase space is combined with a Strang splitting of the continuous and discontinuous mathematical operators governing the moment transport. We verify this CQMOM framework against Monte Carlo simulations of the same particle model for representative test cases of increasing complexity, including drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition, at different Stokes numbers. With two nodes per coordinate, the particle number, the mean size, and the mean aspect ratio agree with the Monte Carlo solution within its statistical uncertainty, and the velocity statistics to within 7 %. Time-step and quadrature resolution studies identify the conditional velocity quadrature as the main source of the remaining deviations, for which we discuss potential remedies. Overall, the results demonstrate that the conditional quadrature representation preserves the geometric-kinematic correlations of the particle population in a five-dimensional phase space, at a cost more than 60 times lower than that of a single Monte Carlo realization.

infographic.key_insight: CQMOM captures coupled size, shape, and velocity distributions of oblate spheroidal particles at over 60 times lower computational cost than a single Monte Carlo realization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports efficient modeling of non-spherical particle transport, breakage, and classification while preserving geometric–kinematic correlations.
method: Represent size, aspect ratio, and three velocity components using conditional quadrature.
Assume particles continuously adopt their drag-maximizing orientation.
Apply Strang splitting to continuous and discontinuous moment-transport operators.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against Monte Carlo tests covering drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition at different Stokes numbers, two nodes per coordinate reproduced particle number and mean geometry within statistical uncertainty, with velocity statistics agreeing to within 7%.
infographic.watch_item: Conditional velocity quadrature is the main source of residual error, and the drag-maximizing orientation assumption restricts the modeled orientation dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: A conditional quadrature method of moments for populations of oblate spheroidal particles

title: The 1/4-power law for bounded variation of wall turbulence from the Kármán-Howarth equation
authors: Xi Chen, Katepalli R. Sreenivasan
abstract: By applying the Kármán-Howarth (KH) equation to turbulent channel flows, we derive the $1/4$-power bounded laws for the peak dissipation and the normalized mean-square streamwise velocity fluctuation. The analysis requires two additional inputs, both standard in the study of turbulent wall flows: the logarithmic mean velocity profile and the near-isotropy of the spatial velocity derivatives. Self-similarity of KH equation yields, for the profile of the mean-square streamwise velocity, the form $c_1 - c_2 (y/δ)^{1/4}$ in the overlap region (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2023), where $δ$ is the half-channel height; it also provides the basis for constructing self-similar profiles for high-order moments of streamwise velocity (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2025). Furthermore, the analysis yields the form $c_1' - c_2' Re^{-1/4}_τ$ for the inner peak of the streamwise mean-square velocity (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2022), and a similar bounded relation for a characteristic wall dissipation (Chen and Sreenivasan, 2021).

infographic.key_insight: The Kármán–Howarth equation yields bounded 1/4-power laws for streamwise velocity variance and dissipation in turbulent channel flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These scaling laws can inform high-Reynolds-number wall-turbulence models by constraining how fluctuation peaks and dissipation approach finite limits.
method: Apply the Kármán–Howarth equation to turbulent channel flow.
Use a logarithmic mean velocity profile and near-isotropy of spatial velocity derivatives.
Derive overlap-region variance scaling as c₁ − c₂(y/δ)^(1/4) and inner-peak scaling as c₁′ − c₂′Re_τ^(−1/4).
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations linked to prior scaling results, but provides no quantitative dataset comparisons or validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Application depends on the validity of the logarithmic-profile and derivative near-isotropy assumptions; extrapolation beyond channel flow requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: The 1/4-power law for bounded variation of wall turbulence from the Kármán-Howarth equation

title: What explainable deep learning reveals about wall-bounded turbulence: insights from conditional surprisal
authors: Belén Reverte-Badillo, Andrés Cremades, Ricardo Vinuesa, Sergio Hoyas
abstract: Explainable deep learning (XDL) has identified regions of wall turbulence important for prediction that are only partly captured by classical coherent-structure criteria. We examine turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers $Re_τ\simeq125$ and $550$ by comparing SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with conditional surprisal, which quantifies how unexpected an observed velocity transition is given its initial state. Although SHAP selection favours energetic fluid and largely overlaps classical masks, selected fluid outside these masks is less energetic but exhibits higher surprisal. Near the wall, at comparable fluctuation energy and wall distance, high-surprisal voxels outside classical masks are approximately 11 and 5 times more likely to be selected by SHAP than low-surprisal voxels, respectively. Within classical masks, the factor is about 1.3. SHAP-selected structures containing paired high- and low-speed regions exhibit surprisal maxima near their internal $u=0$ interfaces, where transverse velocity fluctuations remain nonzero. These interfaces contain vortical and SHAP-only regions, with the latter accounting for more than half of their reconstructed area. In part of the buffer layer, the SHAP-only portions have higher mean surprisal than the vortical portions. However, comparison with generic $u=0$ surfaces indicates that much of the raw interfacial surprisal excess is associated with surrounding fluctuation energy; after energy matching, the equally weighted surface comparison is statistically compatible with unity on the retained common support. Together, these results show how state-conditioned velocity transitions complement instantaneous structure-identification criteria in characterizing SHAP-selected flow.

infographic.key_insight: SHAP-selected turbulent regions outside classical structure masks are less energetic but show more unexpected velocity transitions, revealing predictive information beyond instantaneous coherent structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining SHAP with conditional surprisal could help assess whether turbulence-prediction models capture informative flow dynamics beyond energetic structures.
method: Study turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers Reτ ≈ 125 and 550.
Compare SHAP-selected regions with classical structure masks using state-conditioned velocity-transition surprisal.
Analyze internal u = 0 interfaces and compare surfaces after matching fluctuation energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Near the wall, at comparable fluctuation energy and wall distance, high-surprisal voxels outside classical masks were approximately 11× and 5× more likely to be SHAP-selected at Reτ ≈ 125 and 550, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Raw interfacial surprisal excess is largely associated with surrounding fluctuation energy; after energy matching, the equally weighted surface comparison is statistically compatible with unity on retained common support.
infographic.paper_title: What explainable deep learning reveals about wall-bounded turbulence: insights from conditional surprisal

title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
authors: Zachary T. Hilliard, Amin Chabchoub, Mohammad Farazmand
abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

infographic.key_insight: A single-location wave time series can enable reconstruction of a nonlinear wave field and forecasting of extreme waves driven by self-focusing soliton dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce sensing requirements for monitoring and forecasting extreme waves in settings consistent with its unidirectional wave assumptions.
method: Combine deep learning and compressed sensing to reconstruct waves from sparse observations.
Exploit self-similarity in the unidirectional nonlinear wave evolution equation.
Use reconstructed wave fields to forecast rogue-wave formation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Forecasts based on point observations from controlled water-wave tank experiments showed excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field.
infographic.watch_item: Performance in noisy, multidirectional ocean conditions is not established by the controlled tank results described in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation

title: The role of turbulent jet dynamics on contrail formation from conventional and sustainable aviation fuels
authors: Luca Boscagli, Stelios Rigopoulos, George Papadakis
abstract: Large-eddy simulations (LES) coupled with a discretised population balance equation (PBE) are used to quantify the effect of turbulence on the early stages of contrail formation (jet regime) for both conventional (soot-rich) and sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs). SAFs typically have low aromatic content which causes a shift in the dominant nucleation pathway. The contribution from soot (non-volatile particulate matter, nvPM) is reduced, while the contribution from volatile particulate matter (vPM) is increased. The computational domain reproduces an experimental jet configuration that replicates the thermodynamic conditions encountered in the upper troposphere. The LES-PBE simulations capture well the jet-core cooling and bracket the experimental values of ice-crystal characteristics (number concentration, mean diameter and mass density) if a range of judicious values for parameters not specified in the experiments are employed. With the aid of one-dimensional, one-way coupled PBE approach, it is shown that soot particle activation can be reliably captured using steady aerosol-jet models. On the other hand, volatile particle activation is significantly affected by large fluctuations in temperature and humidity (and thereby supersaturation). Further downstream, non-linear dynamic coupling between the gas and aerosol phases becomes increasingly important for ice-crystal growth as well. Overall, the results demonstrate that for SAFs, turbulence is an important driver of particle activation and subsequent ice crystal growth and cannot be neglected. This finding motivates more fundamental studies to assess how turbulent jet dynamics modulates contrail formation in realistic engine configurations.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent temperature and humidity fluctuations strongly affect volatile-particle activation and subsequent ice-crystal growth, making turbulence essential to modeling early contrails from sustainable aviation fuels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Contrail predictions for low-aromatic aviation fuels should resolve turbulent mixing and gas–aerosol coupling rather than rely solely on steady aerosol-jet models.
method: Large-eddy simulations coupled with a discretised population balance equation.
Experimental jet configuration reproducing upper-tropospheric thermodynamic conditions.
One-dimensional, one-way coupled population-balance modeling to assess activation pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations captured jet-core cooling and bracketed experimental ice-crystal number concentration, mean diameter and mass density across selected values of unspecified parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Unspecified experimental parameters introduce uncertainty, and applicability to realistic engine configurations requires further study.
infographic.paper_title: The role of turbulent jet dynamics on contrail formation from conventional and sustainable aviation fuels

title: Dynamics and stability of volatile thin liquid films on a heated vertical cylinder
authors: Sonam, Souradip Chattopadhyay, Naveen Tiwari
abstract: Volatile thin liquid films flowing down heated vertical cylinders are central to many heat transfer applications, including evaporative condensers, cooling of electronics, and solar thermal systems. Despite their importance, the coupled dynamics of evaporation, thermocapillarity, and interfacial instabilities on cylindrical geometries remain poorly understood. In this work, a lubrication-based model is developed to capture the nonlinear evolution of a volatile thin film under gravity, surface tension, van der Waals forces, and non-conservative evaporative flux. The model incorporates hydrodynamic pressure contributions to evaporation, enabling a unified description of phase-change effects on curved substrates. A linear stability analysis of the model equation is performed with a non-constant base film thickness. The linear growth rate is first obtained for a spatially uniform film. Then, for a spatially nonuniform film, a coupled system of linearized equations is solved using the finite element method. Further, the full liquid-vapor interface is numerically simulated to demonstrate liquid evaporation. Results reveal that evaporation accelerates film thinning, condensation promotes thickening, and van der Waals forces stabilize ultra-thin films by preventing rupture. The influence of Bond number, wavenumber, and pressure-dependent flux laws on droplet formation and collision dynamics is quantified. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into phase-change driven instabilities in cylindrical thin films and have direct implications for the design of efficient thermal management systems, evaporative cooling devices, and surface-engineered heat exchangers.

infographic.key_insight: A lubrication-based model links evaporation, curvature, and interfacial forces to thinning and instability of volatile films on heated vertical cylinders.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings could guide thermal management, evaporative cooling, and heat-exchanger designs that rely on stable liquid-film coverage.
method: Model nonlinear film evolution with gravity, surface tension, van der Waals forces, and pressure-dependent evaporation.
Analyze linear stability for uniform and spatially nonuniform films, using finite elements for the latter.
Numerically simulate liquid–vapor interface evolution and droplet dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Stability analysis and simulations indicate that evaporation accelerates thinning, condensation promotes thickening, and the modeled van der Waals forces prevent ultra-thin-film rupture.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no experimental validation; predictions depend on thin-film assumptions and the chosen evaporation and intermolecular-force laws.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamics and stability of volatile thin liquid films on a heated vertical cylinder

title: Magnetic control of hydrodynamic spin coupling between rotors: Ferrohydrodynamic effects in the two-rotor problem
authors: Efstratios E. Tzirtzilakis
abstract: The hydrodynamic spin coupling between two rotors ("fluid gears") is investigated numerically for a magnetic fluid in non-uniform magnetic fields. An active cylinder drives a torque-free passive one inside a circular corral, with one rotor heated. The model combines magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and ferrohydrodynamics (FHD), with the full Kelvin force and temperature-dependent Langevin magnetisation. For the oil-based ferrofluid EFH1 the Lorentz force is negligible, and the Kelvin force drives thermomagnetic convection from the heated rotor. Steady torque-free states are computed with Taylor-Hood finite elements, the gear ratio $Γ$ being an additional unknown. Without a field the results agree within 1-8% with published planar simulations up to $\mathrm{Re}\approx 50$. About 17,000 steady states cover 34 arrangements of wires, NdFeB rods and magnet cores, gaps $G=0.1$-$0.7$, $\mathrm{Re}=10$-$40$ and heating of 5-20 K. Because the coupling is weak, fields of 1-2 mT change $Γ$ by an amount comparable to $Γ$ itself. At 2 mT it is reversed, strengthened or weakened in nine cases out of ten. The outcome is set by the source position: at the experimental gap and $\mathrm{Re}=20$ a source below the corral or behind the active rotor strengthens the gear-like counter-rotation up to 2.7-fold, and a source above the corral reverses it into belt-like corotation. Several sources do not act additively, and a magnet core inside the active rotor raises $|Γ|$ at small gaps to seven times the largest hydrodynamic value. At fixed geometry and Reynolds number, field strength and heating act approximately through a single thermomagnetic source parameter.

infographic.key_insight: Weak magnetic fields can strengthen, weaken or reverse hydrodynamic coupling between ferrofluid rotors, with source position determining the response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Magnetic placement and heating offer contactless control of fluid-mediated rotor motion, potentially enabling tunable microscale transmissions.
method: Coupled MHD–FHD model with full Kelvin force and temperature-dependent Langevin magnetisation.
Taylor–Hood finite elements solve steady flow and the torque-free passive rotor’s gear ratio.
Swept magnetic-source arrangements, rotor gaps, Reynolds numbers and heating levels.
infographic.evidence_signal: About 17,000 steady states covered 34 source arrangements; zero-field results agreed within 1–8% with published planar simulations, while 2 mT fields altered coupling in nine cases out of ten.
infographic.watch_item: Results are steady numerical predictions for a specific ferrofluid and confined geometry; transient behavior and experimental transfer require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic control of hydrodynamic spin coupling between rotors: Ferrohydrodynamic effects in the two-rotor problem
